title: HypCL: Adapting CLIP in Hyperbolic Space for Continual Learning
claim: Freezing the backbone and composing lightweight task adapters in hyperbolic space, then calibrating logits with prototypes, yields continual adaptation.
layout: Single panel; frozen encoders stacked left, flow rightward to calibration; dashed hyperbolic inset
description: A single wide diagram of the method's architecture. The top peach block is the image encoder and the bottom blue block is the text encoder. Each shows three transformer layers separated by ellipses. Each layer has FFN, Attention and QKV bars. Snowflake icons mark frozen parts. Flame icons mark trainable QKV in the image encoder. A dashed rounded box labeled 'Hyperbolic space' sits in the middle. It holds a task stream D1..Dt feeding grayscale weight matrices, written exp0(WM1) ⊕c ... ⊕c exp0(WMt). On the right, image features pass through a 'project' funnel. Peach circles are prototypes. Green image-feature boxes and blue text-feature boxes feed a green 'Logits Calibration' block through brackets and arrows. The eye goes first to the encoder stacks, then to the central hyperbolic inset, then to the right-hand calibration.
caption: Overview of HypCL. We freeze CLIP and attach task-specific adapters to the visual encoder’s attention projections. Task
abstract: Recently, vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) have been increasingly adopted for continual learning to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. However, existing CLIP-based methods typically freeze the backbone to preserve pre-trained knowledge, which limits the model's ability to learn discriminative features for downstream tasks. In this paper, we introduce HypCL, a parameter-efficient framework that continually adapts CLIP in hyperbolic space for continual learning. Our key insight is that the exponentially expanding capacity of hyperbolic geometry naturally accommodates the growing class space and promotes stronger inter-class separation. Specifically, HypCL attaches task-specific adapters and composes their updates sequentially in the Poincaré ball. To exploit the enhanced feature separability of hyperbolic geometry, HypCL maintains visual prototypes computed from the adapted features, which serve as stable anchors for calibrating predictions at inference. Extensive experiments on standard class-incremental benchmarks demonstrate that HypCL consistently outperforms existing CLIP-based continual learning methods.
